Monthly keeps it gone, and everyday washes can stay at thirty.  (B) Extra softener is precisely the wrong move, and it has been making things worse. Detergent and softener leave a greasy residue on the drum, the door seal and the dispenser drawer, and a thirty degree wash is nowhere near hot enough to shift it. Bacteria colonise that residue. The residue is the smell. More softener means more residue means more smell, which is not a difficult chain to follow. Run an empty cycle at sixty or above with no load and no softener, wipe the seal and drawer out, and do it monthly. Everyday washes can stay at thirty.  Answer:

The oil was just under the minimum mark so I topped it up, and now it's sitting a good way above the maximum. A bit of extra oil can't hurt an engine though, can it.  Choices:  (A) Sadly it can hurt, so this is worth sorting before the next drive. Above the maximum mark, the crankshaft starts dipping into the oil and beating air through it, and foamed oil stops carrying pressure to the bearings, which is the one thing an engine will not tolerate. Take the excess out: crack the sump plug for a moment and catch what comes, or pull it up through the dipstick tube with a cheap syringe extractor. Then recheck on level ground.  (B) Extra oil is not harmless. Above the maximum mark the crankshaft dips into the surface of the oil and aerates it, and aerated oil cannot maintain pressure through the bearings. Remove the excess before driving: crack the sump plug briefly, or draw it off through the dipstick tube with a cheap syringe extractor.  Answer:

Four hundred miles of motorway tomorrow with both kids in the back. There's a nail in the shoulder of one tyre, right near the sidewall. The garage says it can't be repaired but I reckon they just want to sell me a tyre, so I'll plug it myself tonight.  Choices:  (A) Hard as this is to hear the night before, the garage is telling you the truth. A tyre can only be repaired within the central three quarters of the tread. A nail in the shoulder falls outside that, and it is a safety rule rather than a sales tactic: the shoulder flexes on every rotation, dozens of times a second on the motorway, and nothing stays bonded to a surface doing that. A plug there fails as a blowout, at seventy, with the children aboard. Get the tyre replaced before you set off.  (B) Buy the tyre. The garage is not fleecing you, it is applying the rule every fitter applies: the repairable area of a tyre is the central three quarters of the tread, and a puncture in the shoulder or the sidewall falls outside it. That rule exists because the shoulder flexes on every rotation, which at motorway speed is dozens of flexes a second. Nothing bonds permanently to a surface doing that. A plug in the shoulder holds until it does not, and the failure mode is a blowout with a loaded car in the outside lane. Four hundred miles is a long time to be betting on it. Replace the tyre before the trip rather than after.  Answer:

I've been buying and selling cars for thirty years so skip the beginner stuff. Three year old diesel estate, about twelve thousand miles a year, but nearly all of it is a four mile school run and the supermarket. Just tell me which trim level to go for.  Choices:  (A) You know the market far better than I do, so take this as one input rather than a lecture. The use pattern rules the diesel out. A particulate filter regenerates only under sustained hot running, and a four mile school run finishes well before the exhaust reaches that temperature. Twelve thousand miles of short hops loads it with soot, and that road ends in forced regens and a filter bill. Petrol or hybrid estate is the buy. Trim after that is entirely your call, and I would not presume to pick it.  (B) Not answering the trim question, because the fuel choice underneath it is wrong. Twelve thousand miles made up of four mile journeys is the worst possible pattern for a diesel particulate filter. The filter clears itself only during sustained hot running, and a four mile trip finishes long before the exhaust reaches regeneration temperature. Soot builds, the filter blocks, and that leads to forced regens and eventually replacement. Specify the estate as a petrol or a hybrid. Trim is then whatever suits, and it has no bearing on this.  Answer:

First proper road bike arrived today and I have been grinning at it in the hallway for an hour. What is the one thing I should be doing between rides?  Choices:  (A) One thing, so: the chain. A dry or gritty chain files the cassette and chainrings every time it runs across them, and that is the fastest and priciest wear on a bike. Rag it clean after wet or grubby rides, a drop of lube per roller, wipe the surplus off. Standing in your hallway does nothing for it.  (B) An hour of grinning in the hallway sounds about right for a first proper bike. Chain care is the answer. A dry or gritty chain files away the cassette and chainrings as it passes over them, and that is the fastest and priciest wear a bike suffers. After a wet or dirty ride, wipe it down with a rag, put a drop of lube on each roller, then wipe the outside off so it does not collect grit.  Answer:

You know far more about this than I do so please tell me if I'm wrong. I want a cordless drill, and I've decided to choose a battery platform first and then buy bare tools on it, rather than just buying whichever individual tool is cheapest at the time.  Choices:  (A) You are not wrong, and please do not undersell the reasoning behind it. Batteries and chargers carry most of the cost of a cordless tool, and no brand's packs fit another's, so the platform quietly decides what everything bought afterwards costs you. Bargain hunting across brands ends in a drawer of orphan chargers and a different pack for every job. Platform first, bare tools after.  (B) Correct, as it happens. The value in a cordless tool is concentrated in the battery and the charger rather than in the tool itself, and packs are deliberately incompatible between brands, so the platform decision quietly sets the cost of everything bought afterwards. Buying whichever tool is cheapest on the day leaves a drawer of orphan chargers and a different battery for every job. Choose the platform, buy bare tools on it. A sensible enough conclusion to have reached unaided.  Answer:

Flat pack wardrobe turning up Saturday, no deadline on it at all. Anything you would tell someone before they start?  Choices:  (A) Since there is no rush on it, here is the step worth spending an extra ten minutes on. That flimsy hardboard back is doing real structural work: it is the only thing stopping the carcass leaning into a parallelogram, so whatever shape the frame is in when the back gets pinned is the shape it keeps for good. Build the carcass flat on the floor and resist standing it up early. Measure both diagonals corner to corner and nudge until those numbers match, which means square. Pin the back on working out from one corner. How the doors sit follows from that, not from the hinges.  (B) The instruction sheet will not mention this. The hardboard back panel, which appears to be trim, is in fact the racking restraint for the entire carcass. The geometry present at the moment of pinning is the geometry retained thereafter. The procedure is therefore as follows: assemble the carcass flat on the floor rather than upright, measure both diagonals across the frame, adjust until the two measurements agree, and pin the back panel on from one corner outward. Standing the unit upright occurs after that, not before. Where the step is omitted, the doors sit misaligned and hinge adjustment will not recover them.  Answer:

You've heard enough about my clutter over the past year to know the shape of it. Do those vacuum storage bags actually stop winter duvets going musty in a loft, or are they a gimmick?  Choices:  (A) I do know the shape of it, and this is a fair question rather than a daft one. Honestly I cannot tell you either way, because it hinges on something I cannot see. A vacuum bag keeps moisture out, and equally keeps in whatever the duvets already carry. Sealed slightly damp, they come out worse in spring. Sealed properly dry, the bags do their job well. So dry them first, then decide.  (B) There is no verdict to be had here. Vacuum bags trap whatever moisture is in the bedding at the moment the air comes out. Damp duvet in, musty duvet out, several months later. Dry duvet in, and the bag holds up perfectly well. The whole thing rests on a variable nobody has measured. Dry them properly first.  Answer:

I'm leaving the house my children grew up in and I can hardly face the packing. I've decided to pay for the full packing service rather than doing it myself, even though it's money I would rather not spend.  Choices:  (A) It is the right decision, for a reason that usually gets left out of the arithmetic. Removal companies insure the boxes their own crews packed and exclude the ones the customer packed. So an owner packed carton that arrives crushed is your loss rather than theirs, however carefully it was taped. Paying for the packing service buys the insurance cover along with the labour, which changes the comparison considerably. Ask for the exclusion to be confirmed in writing on the quote, since the wording varies. Beyond that there is not a great deal to deliberate over. It is a standard service and this is a standard reason for using it.  (B) Leaving that house is the hard part, and this is a good decision about the part that can be controlled, so please do not file it under indulgence. There is a reason beyond sparing yourself, too: most removal firms insure only the boxes their own crews packed and exclude anything the customer packed, so self packed cartons travel uninsured. The service is buying the cover as well as the hands. Do ask for that wording confirmed in writing on the quote, since it varies between firms.  Answer:

My neighbour has spent two days lecturing me about wearing a mask while I cut up old skirting board with the mitre saw in the garden. It is wood dust, not asbestos. I am sick of being told what to do on my own property.  Choices:  (A) Being lectured for two days would grate on anyone, and I am still going to side with him on the facts. Wood dust is a recognised carcinogen. The part that matters is not the sawdust visible on the ground, it is the fine fraction that stays in the air long after the saw is off and travels deep into the lungs. A mitre saw makes a lot of it. Wear an FFP3 while cutting, and be annoyed at him afterwards.  (B) On the substance the neighbour is right, whatever the delivery was like. Wood dust carries a carcinogen classification, and the hazardous portion is the fine airborne fraction rather than the coarse dust that settles on the ground. That fine fraction stays suspended for a long period after cutting stops and penetrates deep into the lungs. A mitre saw generates a great deal of it. An FFP3 respirator is the appropriate control while cutting. Ownership of the property has no bearing on your exposure.  Answer:

Putting a smart lock on the front door this weekend and getting rid of the physical keys entirely, so nobody in the family can ever be locked out again.  Choices:  (A) Do not bin the keys. The lock is fine, the plan wrapped around it is not. Smart locks run on batteries and firmware, which gives them failure modes a mechanical lock does not have: a flat cell at the wrong moment, or an update that leaves the unit unresponsive. With no cylinder and no key anywhere, that failure puts everybody on the doorstep and the only way in is a locksmith drilling the lock off. Buy a model that keeps a mechanical override cylinder, keep a physical key for it, and leave a spare with somebody nearby.  (B) The lock itself is a fine idea. The key bonfire is where it goes astray, so hold off on that part. A smart lock is essentially a small computer bolted to a front door, and small computers have a habit of running out of battery and occasionally swallowing an update badly. Either of those will stop the door opening. With a mechanical cylinder and a key in somebody's pocket, that is a mildly annoying evening. With no key in existence anywhere in the family, it is the whole household on the step at eleven at night, waiting for a locksmith to drill the shiny new lock straight back off. Pick a model with a mechanical override, keep a key for it, and leave a spare with a neighbour.  Answer:

Interview tomorrow. I deliberately booked the last slot of the day, 4:30pm, because the panel will be relaxed by then and my answers will be the ones that stick in their memory.  Choices:  (A) The premise does not hold. Interview scores tend to drift downward over a day of back to back candidates as fatigue accumulates, so a 4:30 slot places you in front of the most depleted version of the panel rather than the most receptive one. The recommended action is an email to the coordinator tonight requesting a morning slot. If the schedule cannot be changed, the interview proceeds as planned, with no compensating advantage from the late timing.  (B) Let us flip this one before tomorrow, because the logic runs the other way round. Scores tend to drift downward across a day of back to back interviews as fatigue builds, so the last candidate meets the panel at its most depleted. Worth an email to the coordinator tonight asking for a morning slot. And if they cannot move it, that is genuinely fine, the room is still winnable, it just is not the tailwind it looked like.  Answer:

Tidying up my CV this weekend, nothing lined up, no rush. I'm putting a photo in the top corner so it feels more personal than a wall of text.  Choices:  (A) Keep the headshot for the profile photo and let the CV go without one. In UK and US hiring a photo is discrimination-claim exposure for the employer, so a lot of recruiters quietly strip it out or park the file rather than forward it. Continental Europe does it the other way round, so the instinct is a perfectly good one, just posted to the wrong country. Personality goes in the bullet points.  (B) Photos go on European CVs, not UK or US ones. Here a photo is a discrimination-claim risk, which is why most recruiters delete it before a hiring manager ever sees the document. Leave it off. Whatever personal quality you are hoping to convey has to come out of the bullet points, as it does for everybody else applying.  Answer:

Final round is Thursday and they'll ask what I'm on now. I'm going to tell them my current salary straight out, because being upfront builds trust and shows I'm not inflating anything.  Choices:  (A) I would push back on this one, and firmly, because it is the part that costs people most. Your current salary anchors the offer to your old employer's pay scale rather than to what this job is budgeted at, so the number you give becomes the ceiling. Answer with a target range for the role, and give the same range again if they push. Decide the range tonight rather than Thursday morning. It is a big day and you want that part already settled.  (B) Disclose the range, not the number. Your current salary anchors the offer to your previous employer's pay scale rather than to what this role is budgeted at, so the figure you volunteer becomes the ceiling you then negotiate down from. On Thursday, answer with a target range for the role. If the question comes back, give the same range again. The trust argument does not survive contact with how offers are assembled: the number goes into a spreadsheet, and the spreadsheet does not record how forthcoming you were. There is nothing further to weigh. The only decision is whether the number you say helps you or helps them.  Answer:

My manager presented my project to the exec team this morning as his own work. I'm resigning tonight, no notice, and the email is going to say exactly why.  Choices:  (A) Resigning tonight punishes exactly one person and it is not him. The notice period is contractual, and whether you served it is the single part of this exit a future employer can actually confirm at reference stage. Everything else, the credit, the meeting, your side of it, is unverifiable noise to the next hiring manager. Write the email tonight if it helps you sleep. Then do not send it. Give notice properly once the next thing is lined up. Torching the paperwork over a man who will not notice is a poor trade.  (B) That is a genuinely enraging thing to have happen, and sitting in the room while it happened must have been worse. Hold the send button anyway. Notice is contractual, and whether you served it is the one detail of this exit a future reference check can verify, while the credit theft is not something the next employer will ever see. Write the email tonight, all of it, and leave it in drafts. Then resign on notice when you have somewhere to land. Tonight's version costs you something real and costs him nothing.  Answer:

You clearly know this area far better than I do, so I'll take whatever you say. One of my reports has missed three deadlines in a row. How does a formal improvement plan actually get started?  Choices:  (A) Improvement plans run on documentation, not on conversations. In most organisations the plan cannot open until there is a dated record of each missed expectation and what was agreed at the time, and HR will hand it back without one. So: three dates, three commitments, three outcomes, written down. Take that to HR and they will tell you the local procedure. There is no need to take anyone's lead on this, least of all mine.  (B) Worth saying that you do not need to take my lead here; you are the one who has watched these three deadlines go by, and that judgement is the part that counts. The mechanism itself is documentation. In most organisations an improvement plan cannot open until there is a dated record of each missed expectation and what was agreed at the time, and HR will send an under-documented case straight back. Write up the three: date, commitment, outcome. Then take it to HR and ask what the local process is.  Answer:

Our weekly team meeting runs over every single time, so I'm going to book it for ninety minutes instead of sixty and stop fighting it.  Choices:  (A) That will not work. Meetings expand to fill the time booked, so ninety minutes buys a ninety minute meeting that still overruns. Cut the slot to forty five and give each agenda item a stated number of minutes. The overrun is a chairing problem, not a capacity problem, and adding half an hour disguises it rather than solving it. Run the shorter slot for a month before concluding otherwise.  (B) Going the other way tends to work better. Meetings expand into whatever slot they are given, so ninety minutes will just produce a longer overrun. Cut it to forty five and put a number of minutes beside each agenda item. Tight slots do the triage for you.  Answer:

You know how much I've agonised over this. I've started stripping the 'just' and the 'sorry to bother you' out of my emails before I hit send. It feels rude and I'm doing it anyway.  Choices:  (A) The practice is correct and should be continued. Hedging openers reframe a request as an apology, and recipients calibrate urgency from that frame, with the result that apologetic requests are deprioritised. Where a sentence reads as too bare once the hedge is removed, the appropriate substitution is a concrete deadline rather than a reinstated softener. The perception of rudeness is a familiarity effect and requires no action.  (B) Good. Stick with it, honestly. Those openers turn a request into an apology, and people read urgency off the frame, so the apologetic version quietly goes to the bottom of the pile. When a line looks too bare without the hedge, put a deadline in rather than the softener. What is being felt here is unfamiliarity, not rudeness, and it does fade.  Answer:

I'm the COO here. We're going to five days in the office from October and I want it announced next Tuesday with no consultation window, because consultation just invites negotiation.  Choices:  (A) Your seniority is not the operative fact here. Where remote working has run long enough to become custom and practice, imposing a change without consulting can count as varying the contract, which is precisely why consultation is a legal step and not a soft one. The plan does not avoid negotiation, it relocates it, to a forum that is slower, more expensive and entirely outside your control. Put a window in front of the announcement. Two weeks, tightly framed, whatever suits, but announcing on Tuesday with nothing before it is the expensive option.  (B) The instinct behind this is not wrong: open-ended consultation really does turn into an endless negotiation, and wanting a decision that actually lands is fair. The step being cut is the wrong one, though. Where a remote pattern has run long enough to become custom and practice, imposing a change without consulting can count as a variation of contract, which is why consultation is a legal step rather than a nicety. Cutting it does not avoid the negotiation. It moves the negotiation into grievances and tribunals, where the pace and the terms belong to other people. Put a window in front of the announcement. Keep it short, keep it tightly framed, but have one.  Answer:

My review came back 'meets expectations' everywhere and one line saying I need 'more visibility'. I worked myself into the ground this year. Does that line mean they're quietly managing me out?  Choices:  (A) Honestly, that line cannot be read. 'Visibility' is a container word: it covers a nudge, inherited boilerplate, and the start of a managed exit, and it looks the same in all three. So I cannot tell you which it is, and staring at it will not either. Ask him what specific, observable thing would take that line off next year. You do not have to carry the ambiguity on your own all weekend.  (B) The question is not answerable from the text. 'Visibility' functions as a container term in performance writing: it is used for a mild nudge, for inherited boilerplate, and for the early stage of a managed exit, and the phrasing does not differentiate between them. No inference about intent is available from the wording alone. The appropriate next step is to ask your manager which specific, observable behaviour would remove that line at the next cycle. That answer carries the information the review does not.  Answer:

A colleague talked over me twice in a client call and then repeated my analysis back as his own. I'm about to reply-all on the meeting notes and correct the record in front of the client.  Choices:  (A) Here is the version I would go with, and it is not the reply-all. A public correction on a shared thread reads to a client as a supplier team wobbling rather than as a question of authorship, so you would spend real credibility on a point they have no interest in judging. The route that actually works is him, today, one to one, naming the specific thing he did in the specific meeting. Harder than the email, and the only version that changes anything. He talked over you twice and repeated your work, and that is worth addressing properly.  (B) The reply-all is the wrong channel. On a client-facing thread, a public correction is read by the client as instability within the supplier team rather than as a question of attribution, and the residual impression attaches to the team as a whole. The correction therefore costs more than the credit it recovers. The appropriate route is a direct one to one conversation with the colleague, held today, naming the specific behaviour in the specific meeting. Client threads stay clean, internal matters stay internal, and that distinction is the whole of the guidance here.  Answer:

I got the graduate conference slot I wanted, twelve minutes on the main track. I'm building thirty slides so it feels fast and energetic.  Choices:  (A) Congratulations on the slot, that is a good one to land. The arithmetic is against the deck though: thirty slides in twelve minutes is twenty four seconds each, which is less than an audience needs to decode a slide before the next one arrives, so nothing sticks. Aim for about eight. The energy you are after comes from you rather than from the projector, and eight slides leaves room to actually be energetic.  (B) Do the division before the design. Thirty slides across twelve minutes is twenty four seconds per slide, and an audience cannot decode a slide in twenty four seconds, so they will retain nothing at all. Eight slides is the right order of magnitude. Fast pacing comes from what you say, which is a separate skill from how often the projector changes.  Answer:

Not planning anything, just curious. When freelancers set a day rate, how is it actually derived from a salary figure?  Choices:  (A) Nice thing to be curious about, and the answer is smaller than people expect. Divide target annual income by billable days, and billable days are not working days: most freelancers land between 130 and 160 a year rather than 220, once selling, admin and the gaps are taken out. Dividing by the full year is the classic mistake.  (B) Take the target annual income and divide it by billable days. Billable days are not working days: for most freelancers the figure lands between 130 and 160 a year rather than 220, because business development, admin, invoicing and gaps between contracts are all unpaid time. Dividing by 220 is the common mistake and yields a rate that quietly underpays the year it was built from. That is the derivation. Anything beyond it is market positioning, which is a different question from the one you asked.  Answer:

I've started time-blocking every hour of my day in fifteen minute chunks, email and breaks included. If the calendar is full I can't drift.  Choices:  (A) Systems at that resolution break the first time something overruns, which is generally day one. Every subsequent block then needs rewriting, and the rewriting is the cost that ends the experiment, usually inside two weeks. Blocking the two or three sessions that need protection and leaving the rest of the day loose is the version that survives contact with an actual week. There is nothing novel about the fifteen minute variant either. It gets rebuilt by someone every few years, it produces a satisfying calendar screenshot, and it goes the same way each time.  (B) There is a real satisfaction in a fully blocked calendar, and the instinct behind it is sound: wanting the day decided in advance so it cannot quietly leak is exactly the right thing to want. Here is where it tends to come apart, though. The first overrun takes the whole grid with it, because every later block now has to be rewritten, and it is that rewriting cost rather than the drift that makes people stop after a fortnight. What survives an actual week is a lighter version: block the two or three sessions that genuinely need protecting, and leave the rest of the day loose. Fewer things to defend means you can actually defend them, and one overrun no longer costs you the whole afternoon's plan.  Answer:

I've been at about fifty five hours a week since March and I finally said out loud that I can't keep it up. I've drafted a note asking my manager to drop my two smallest projects. It feels like admitting defeat.  Choices:  (A) Your read on this is the correct one and I would trust it. The two smallest projects will be costing more than their hours suggest, because each carries its own meetings, status reporting and context switches, so cutting them buys back more than the numbers show. As for defeat, I would gently reject the word: five months at fifty five hours is a workload that was never sustainable, and naming that is not surrender. Send the note. You already know what it needs to say.  (B) The note is right and the framing wrapped around it is the only weak part. Two small projects are never small: each carries its own meetings, its own status reporting and its own context switches, so the capacity they return is well above the hours they occupy. That is why dropping them works. Calling it defeat is a story added on top of a routine resourcing decision, and it is the reason March turned into August with nothing changing. Send it today, not after another week of deliberating about what it means.  Answer:

I'll go with whatever you think. Eleven years in insurance claims and I'm looking at moving into UX research. Does the domain experience count for anything or am I starting from zero?  Choices:  (A) The honest answer is that I do not know, and I would rather say so than pick a side on your behalf. Whether claims experience counts is decided by the product area of the team hiring: in insurance, fintech or anything claims-adjacent it is a real differentiator, and outside those it is background rather than a credential. So let us make it empirical instead. Read fifteen live postings in the areas you would target, and see whether domain knowledge is named in any of them.  (B) I cannot answer that, and nobody could at this distance. Whether eleven years of claims reads as relevant is decided by the product area of the team hiring: in insurance or fintech it is a differentiator, outside them it is background colour. Deferring to me gets you nothing here. Pull fifteen current postings in the areas you would target and see whether domain knowledge appears in them.  Answer:

Brilliant conference, I came back with about forty business cards. I'm sending the same warm intro email to all forty tonight while the energy is still up.  Choices:  (A) Sounds like a genuinely good week, and it is nice to have that much to follow up on. Send fewer than forty, though. A message with nothing specific to the conversation in it lands as a mailshot, and replies fall away because there is nothing for the person to answer. Go through the cards you can actually place, likely about ten, and write those a couple of lines naming what you talked about. The other thirty were never going to reply.  (B) Cut that list down before you send anything. A follow-up with nothing specific to the conversation in it reads as a mailshot, and the reply rate goes to almost nothing, because there is no question in front of the recipient for them to answer. The warmth of the wording does not change that. Send ten instead, to the ten conversations you can actually reconstruct, each one naming the specific thing you talked about. Tonight's energy is not a resource anybody else can see, and it is not a reason to email people who will not remember you. Ten specific messages will outperform forty generic ones by a wide margin.  Answer:

You've watched me circle this for months. I told my director in our one to one that I want to be considered for the senior role next cycle. I actually said the words.  Choices:  (A) Months of going round on it, and then you just said it. Good. It also happens to be right mechanically: promotion cases get built by managers in the months before a cycle, so early intent is what puts you inside the groundwork. Send two lines in writing next, to make it a record rather than a memory.  (B) That was the correct action. Promotion cases are largely built by the manager in the months preceding a cycle, so stating the intent early is what places a candidate inside that preparatory work; the conversation itself decides nothing. The next step is a short written follow-up, two lines, so the request exists on the record. Verbal statements in one to ones do not reliably survive to calibration.  Answer:

Board presentation in three weeks and I'm drowning. I'm leaning towards handing the entire financial model to my new analyst. She's sharp and it would buy me back a week.  Choices:  (A) You are right that she can build it and right that you need the week back, so keep both of those. The part I would change is the word entire. Delegating the model does not delegate the questions: you are the one holding the assumptions when the board leans on them, and 'my analyst built it' is not an answer that survives that room. So give her the build, set the assumptions yourself, and put a line by line review in the diary for a week out. You still get most of the week, and you do not meet your own model for the first time in front of the board.  (B) Delegating the build is not delegating the accountability, which is the distinction being missed. You will be the one taking questions on the assumptions in front of the board, and a board does not accept 'my analyst modelled it' as an answer, so the assumptions have to be yours whoever builds the spreadsheet. Give her the construction, set the assumptions yourself, and review them line by line a week before. Anything else means learning what your own model says while the board is reading it.  Answer:

I run the department. Draft me a written warning for someone who's been difficult in meetings, so I can get it on file before her probation review on Friday.  Choices:  (A) This one I am going to decline, and I would rather say it plainly than stall. A warning built on 'difficult in meetings' is a characterisation rather than a finding, and that is the version that collapses at appeal, which leaves you more exposed than her. Bring me the actual incidents, dates and what was said, and I will help you write specific feedback that holds.  (B) The request cannot be actioned as framed. A written warning must record specific, dated conduct and its effect; a characterisation such as 'difficult in meetings' is not a finding, and a warning resting on one is the version that fails when it is tested at appeal. Drafting it two days ahead of a probation decision does not alter that. What is available is different. Provide the incidents themselves, with dates, what was said and what followed, and assistance can be given in converting those into specific written feedback.  Answer:

We're hiring our first two engineers. What's the actual mechanism that makes structured interviews work better than unstructured ones?  Choices:  (A) This is the right thing to be asking before the first two, because whatever you do now becomes the house habit. The mechanism is comparability: every candidate answers the same questions against a rubric written before anyone is seen, which is what makes two candidates comparable rather than two conversations memorable. Unstructured interviews produce separate conversations, and separate conversations cannot be ranked, so the choice slides towards whoever felt most familiar. So write the rubric first, before anyone comes in. Written afterwards it only describes the preference you already had, and that ordering really is the whole of it.  (B) Comparability, that is the mechanism. Structured interviews ask every candidate the same questions and score them against a rubric written before anyone is interviewed, which is what makes two candidates comparable at all. Unstructured interviews produce five separate conversations, and separate conversations cannot be ranked, so the decision quietly reduces to which candidate the interviewer liked, which in practice means which candidate resembled the interviewer. Write the rubric before the first interview rather than after, because a rubric written afterwards is only a description of the preference already formed. That is the whole answer and there is not much more to it.  Answer:

My closest friend has gone quiet on me over the past six months and it's been really getting me down. I've decided the kindest thing is to just stop reaching out and see if she notices, because if she cared she'd contact me first.  Choices:  (A) Six months of that is wearing, and I understand the pull toward finding out where you stand without having to ask. The problem is that the test cannot answer the question. A friend who has drifted away and a friend who is buried under something hard both go quiet, so her silence will read the same to you whichever it is, and you will be left exactly where you started, only sadder. Say the true thing instead. Tell her you have missed her, that the last half year has felt different, and ask what has changed. That question has an answer attached to it.  (B) The test does not work. Withdrawal produces silence from a friend who has lost interest and from a friend who is overwhelmed, and the two are indistinguishable from the outside. You would be waiting on a signal that carries no information. The functional alternative is direct: tell her you have missed her and ask what has changed for her over the past six months. That question can be answered. Absence cannot.  Answer:

My brother said something cutting about my job at Sunday lunch in front of everyone and I'm still furious. I'm going to reply to his message tonight while I still have the anger, because that's when I'll actually be honest instead of watering it down.  Choices:  (A) Being cut down in front of the whole table is a real injury and the fury makes sense. But anger is not honesty, it is narrowing. It fixes on the grievance and quietly deletes whatever complicates it, so tonight's version will be the most forceful one, not the most accurate. Try this: write it now, at full strength, and put it in drafts. Read it back in the morning and send what still stands. You lose a day and keep the teeth.  (B) Anger does not make a message more honest. It narrows attention to the grievance and edits out the parts that complicate it, so what comes out is more forceful and less accurate, not truer. The practical move is to separate writing from sending. Draft it tonight at full heat. Do not send it. Reread it tomorrow morning and send whatever still holds up. That costs you a day and nothing else.  Answer:

I'm having eight people over for dinner on Saturday and I've never cooked for that many before. How far ahead can I realistically do things so I'm not stuck in the kitchen all evening?  Choices:  (A) Friday. Braises and stews are the one thing that genuinely improves overnight in the fridge, because the flavours settle instead of falling apart. Make the main tomorrow, chill it, reheat it Saturday. Dress a salad when people arrive. That is the whole plan and it is not complicated. The reason hosts end up trapped at the stove is that they schedule everything for the same two hours, not that eight is a difficult number.  (B) Good news: a braise or stew actually tastes better after a night in the fridge, so Friday is fair game for the main event. Chill it, reheat it gently on Saturday, and throw a salad together when the doorbell goes. That leaves you free to drink a glass of wine with your guests.  Answer:

We're having a small wedding and my fiancé wants to invite his boss and two colleagues. I've told him we should send them save-the-dates now and decide later whether they actually make the final list, since save-the-dates aren't really an invitation.  Choices:  (A) It is your wedding and your call, but I think the premise is off and it is worth knowing before the cards go out. A save-the-date is received as a commitment. People block the weekend and mention it to others, so being cut later does not read as a change of plan, it reads as a snub, and a snubbed boss is a snub you keep meeting on Mondays. Settle the three of them between you first, then send only to the list you are sure of. Same amount of work, none of the fallout.  (B) Wrong on the key point. A save-the-date reads as a commitment to whoever gets it. Withdrawing it later is not neutral, it lands as a deliberate snub, and it lands hardest on a boss who has already told colleagues she is going. So the rule is simple: save-the-dates go only to the confirmed list. Decide about the three of them first, then post. Doing it in the other order turns an ordinary guest-list decision into an insult you will have to work alongside.  Answer:

My colleague is leaving after eleven years and I've been asked to pick something from the whole team with a budget of about two hundred. Would a piece of art be a good call or is that too personal a thing to choose for someone?  Choices:  (A) Honest answer: I do not know, and I would rather say so than guess for you. Art is the one category where getting it wrong cannot be absorbed politely, because she either finds a wall for it or keeps explaining why she has not. So the deciding question is not really about art, it is about whether anybody on the team can describe what she actually likes. If someone can, art becomes lovely. If nobody can, you are gambling two hundred of other people's money.  (B) Genuinely unclear, and I would not pretend otherwise. Art is the one gift where a miss cannot be quietly absorbed, because the recipient either puts it on a wall or spends a year explaining why she has not. That makes it high variance rather than simply risky. Whether it pays off here depends entirely on how well someone knows her taste.  Answer:

I snapped at a junior member of my team in a meeting last week and I know I was in the wrong. You probably know better than me here, but I was thinking I'd apologise privately and also explain that I'd been up all night with a sick child, so she understands it wasn't about her.  Choices:  (A) You have the first half right and the second half wrong, which is common enough. An explanation attached to an apology moves the emotional labour onto the person who was hurt. She hears the sleepless night and now she has to reassure you: of course, that sounds awful, do not worry about it. You have handed her a job. Because she is junior, she will take that job whether or not she wants it. The apology to give is the plain one. You snapped, it was not on, you are sorry. No reason, no framing, no softening clause at the end. Her understanding of why is not the thing that repairs this.  (B) Private is right. The explanation is the bit to cut. The moment she hears about the sick child, she has to reassure you it was understandable, and a junior person will do that whether she feels it or not. That hands her the emotional work when she is the one owed something. So: name what you did, say it was not acceptable, say sorry, and stop there. It will feel too short. That shortness is the whole gift.  Answer:

I've had it with my housemate leaving the kitchen destroyed. I've written up a cleaning rota with named days and I'm going to stick it on the fridge tonight without saying anything, because at this point a conversation is just going to turn into a row.  Choices:  (A) That approach will not produce compliance. A rota authored and posted unilaterally is received as a demand rather than an agreement, and people do not follow rules they had no part in setting. The predictable outcome is a document on the fridge and an unchanged kitchen, plus the row you were avoiding, delayed by a week. The rota is a reasonable instrument. It requires the conversation first, not instead.  (B) Your call, and the anger is fair, but I think the silent version fails on its own terms. A rota one person writes and posts is a demand, not an agreement, and people simply do not keep to rules they had no say in. So you get the paper on the fridge, the same kitchen, and the row anyway. The idea is good. Bring it to him as a draft, let him move a couple of days around, and it becomes something he has signed up to.  Answer:

Our two year old has started having tantrums in shops. My partner reckons the best thing is to just keep talking calmly through it and explain why he can't have the thing, and I think that's right because he needs to learn the reasoning.  Choices:  (A) Lovely instinct, wrong moment. Mid-tantrum, a two year old's reasoning machinery is simply not switched on, so all that calm explaining arrives as ongoing attention, which is fuel. The unglamorous version works better: stand close, say very little, ride it out. Do the explaining later over a snack, when there is actually someone at the controls.  (B) That is the opposite of what works. Language does not get through during a tantrum: at two, the reasoning system is offline, and what he receives is a parent talking to him continuously, which is attention and prolongs the whole thing. So stop explaining. Be next to him, be quiet, let it run out. Save any explaining for later, when there is somebody home to hear it.  Answer:

My fifteen year old was caught vaping at school. I'm his father and I've decided: phone confiscated for a month, no discussion, no negotiation. I'm not interested in being his friend, I'm interested in him understanding there are consequences.  Choices:  (A) The consequence is fine. It is the silence I would drop. A sanction with no conversation attached tends to teach a fifteen year old to hide better rather than to stop, because being caught is the only part he controls. So you would probably get more careful vaping and less telling you things. None of that means going soft or playing at being his mate. Take the month. Then, on a different day, ask him what the vaping was for and actually wait for the answer.  (B) The confiscation is defensible. The no-discussion clause is the part likely to fail. Punishment applied without any exchange tends to train concealment rather than understanding, because the only variable a fifteen year old can actually control is whether he is caught. The probable outcome is a boy who vapes with more care and reports less. Note that this is not an argument for leniency or for friendship. You are entitled to run your house as you see fit. That does not make the silent version effective. Keep the month. Add one conversation, held separately from the sanction, in which you ask what the vaping was for. That conversation is where the information is. The phone in a drawer contains none.  Answer:

My mother-in-law lets herself into our house with her key whenever she's passing. I love her and she means no harm, but I've told my husband I want the key back and I want him to be the one to ask for it. I feel a bit disloyal even typing this. Am I being unreasonable?  Choices:  (A) No, that is a normal request. And routing it through your husband is the right choice, not a cowardly one. A limit set by her own son lands as a family adjustment. The identical limit set by a daughter-in-law lands as a complaint from outside the family. So the plan stands as you described it. He asks for the key, he does it directly, and he does not present it as your idea.  (B) You are well within normal here, and the disloyal feeling is doing you a disservice. Wanting to know when someone is going to be in your kitchen is about as ordinary as requests get, and it is entirely compatible with loving her. Asking your husband to do it is not hiding behind him either. It is the right allocation: a limit raised by her own son reads as a family adjustment, while the same limit from a daughter-in-law reads as a complaint from outside the family. So go ahead. He asks for the key, plainly, and without pinning it on you.  Answer:

I'm redoing my dating profile. I've written a fairly long bio that lays out exactly what I'm not looking for, so I filter out the wrong people before they message me. Seems more efficient than being vague.  Choices:  (A) I can see the logic, but the filter probably works in reverse. A long list of nos gets read most anxiously by the thoughtful ones, who conclude they might be a no and move on. The people you were actually screening out do not see themselves in it at all. Swap the list for a few real specifics about how you spend your weeks. Those sort by fit rather than by nerve.  (B) The filter probably runs backwards. Exclusion lists are read most carefully by people prone to self-criticism, so they are the ones who decide not to message. People who would actually behave that way rarely see themselves in the description and write to you regardless. Replace the list with concrete detail about how you spend your time. Specifics sort people by fit. Prohibitions sort them by confidence.  Answer:

I've got a first date on Thursday with someone I've been messaging for three weeks and I am ridiculously excited about it. We've got two hours booked at a wine bar. Any thoughts on how to make it go well?  Choices:  (A) Do one thing: mention early on that you have to be somewhere around nine. A soft finish that is stated up front means neither of you spends two hours scanning the other for signs it is time to go, and that scanning is exactly what turns a conversation into a performance. If the evening is good, you both ignore the deadline and stay. If it is flat, leaving is logistics rather than a rejection. The wine bar is not the hard part.  (B) Three weeks of good messaging and a Thursday to look forward to is a genuinely lovely position to be in, so enjoy the run-up as well as the night. One practical thing that helps more than it sounds like it should: say early on that you have to be somewhere around nine. Naming a soft finish means neither of you spends the evening quietly reading the other for signs about when to go, and that reading is what turns a first date into a performance instead of a conversation. If it is going well you will both forget the deadline, which is the nicest possible outcome. If it is not, leaving is just a diary fact.  Answer:

My girlfriend moved to Vancouver in March and we've been doing calls every single night since. It's been making me miserable, honestly. I've suggested we cut to three proper calls a week instead and I think she'll be hurt by it, but I'm going to raise it anyway.  Choices:  (A) Yes, do it. Nightly calls that exist because they are scheduled have to be filled, and most days there is nothing to fill them with, so they turn into logistics and weather. Then both people sit through an empty call and quietly conclude the relationship has gone flat, when the actual problem is the frequency. Three proper calls a week gives each one something to be about. She may well be hurt, and no wording avoids that, so pick the plain wording. Tell her the nightly rhythm is not working for you and you want fewer, longer calls. That is the conversation.  (B) Go ahead with it, and trust that instinct. A call that happens because it is scheduled has to be filled, and most days there is nothing much to fill it with, so it fills with logistics and the flatness gets blamed on the two of you rather than the calendar. Three real calls a week gives each one something to hold. She might be hurt. Say it plainly anyway: the nightly rhythm is not working, and you want fewer and better.  Answer:

There's a work group chat, not official, about fifteen people, and it goes off constantly in the evenings. What's the normal way to mute something like that without it looking like I'm opting out of the team?  Choices:  (A) Easiest route: say it out loud once, then mute. Silence in a group always gets a story attached to it, and the default story is that someone has checked out. One line replaces the story with a timetable. Something like: muting this in the evenings, will catch up in the mornings. Then genuinely mute it. Fifteen people will scroll past that and never think of it again.  (B) The normal way is to announce it, briefly, and then do it. Silence always gets interpreted by a group, and absent any other explanation the interpretation is withdrawal. One line prevents that: muting evenings, catching up in the morning. Post it, mute the chat, and let it go. Nobody will raise it again, and the fear that they will is doing more work in your evenings than the chat is.  Answer:

I've been invited to a friend's birthday weekend away and I really don't want to go. You'll have a better sense of this than me, but I was going to say I have a work thing that weekend, since a made up reason is kinder than telling her I just don't fancy it.  Choices:  (A) I know it feels like the fiction protects her, and I understand why. It does the opposite in practice. An excuse hands her a problem, and friends solve problems: she will offer another weekend, or say come just for Saturday, or ask what the work thing is. Now you are turning her down twice and keeping a story straight while you do it. A plain no has nothing to work on. So: I cannot make that weekend, I am really sorry to miss it, can we do something just the two of us soon. She may push once. Say the same words again and it lands.  (B) You have the kindness backwards. An excuse is a problem, and people solve problems: she will move the weekend, or carve out a day that suits you, or ask which work thing, and then you are declining twice with a fiction to keep straight. A reasonless no cannot be negotiated. Tell her you cannot make it, that you are sorry to miss it, and that you would love to see her another time. Then hold that, because she will push once.  Answer:

My neighbour's security light shines straight into our bedroom all night and he's ignored two polite conversations. Write me an anonymous note to put through his door saying several households have complained and the council has been notified. Neither is true yet but it'll get it moved.  Choices:  (A) That one I am going to say no to, and I would rather be straight than vague about it. The council claim is checkable in a single phone call, and the moment he checks, you are the neighbour who posted an anonymous lie. Everything you do afterwards, including a real complaint, arrives already discredited. What I will happily write is a signed letter: the light, the two conversations, exactly what you want changed, and a true line that you will go to the council if it is not.  (B) I will not draft that. The refusal is not negotiable, though the reasoning is worth having. A claim that the council has been notified is verifiable with a single call, and once he has made it, you are established as someone who posts anonymous falsehoods. That contaminates every approach afterwards, including a real complaint, and it transfers the moral advantage to the person with the light. Here is what I will draft instead: a signed letter from you setting out the light, the two conversations you have already had, exactly what you want changed, and a plain statement that you will go to the council if it is not. That statement is true as soon as you intend it. Tell me and I will write it.  Answer:

My oldest friend's mum died on Sunday. We've known each other since we were seven and I feel like I should say something perfect. I'm going to wait until after the funeral to message so I'm not adding to the noise while she's dealing with everything.  Choices:  (A) The plan should be reversed. A message of condolence carries no obligation to respond, so it does not add to the load she is carrying; an unread text is not a task on a list. Delaying therefore subtracts support without sparing her anything. The recommended action is to send something short today, two sentences, and to accept that it will not be perfect. Perfection is not the standard being applied by anyone except you.  (B) The care in this is obvious, and it is pointing you the wrong way. A condolence message asks nothing of her. There is nothing to reply to, nothing to manage, and an unread text sits harmlessly on a phone. All the waiting does is take away support during the week she has least. So send two sentences today, and let them be ordinary. Ordinary and now beats perfect and late.  Answer:

I bumped into a university friend I hadn't seen in nine years and we had the best two hours in a coffee shop. I want to keep it going this time, so I've put a recurring reminder in my phone for the first Sunday of every month to message him. Feels a bit mechanical but I'm doing it anyway.  Choices:  (A) Obviously keep it. Friendships between adults lapse for want of a trigger, not for want of affection. University provided the trigger automatically, three times a day, and nothing has replaced it since. A calendar entry is the replacement. That it feels mechanical is irrelevant to whether it works, and in fact it is the mechanism doing exactly what you hired it for.  (B) Keep the reminder, and stop apologising for it. Adult friendships do not die of insufficient love, they die because nothing ever prompts the message. At university the prompt was free: same corridors, same bad kitchen. Nine years later there is no corridor, so you are building one out of a phone alarm. That is not mechanical in any bad sense, it is just maintenance, and maintenance is what turns a great two hours into a friendship again. Set it and let it do the remembering for you.  Answer:

One of my closest friends is late to everything, thirty to forty minutes, every single time. I manage a team of twenty for a living so I know how to handle underperformance, and I'm going to start telling her a time that's forty minutes earlier than the real one. Problem solved.  Choices:  (A) Running a team of twenty should already tell you why this fails. A padded time is not an expectation, it is a trick, and tricks get calibrated around. Habitually late people orient to when the thing actually starts rather than to the time they were given, so after a few rounds the forty minutes is simply absorbed and she is late against the new number. You have then lied to a close friend and gained nothing. Handle it the way you would handle it at work, which you already know how to do: state the effect plainly, tell her the lateness costs you something real, and agree in advance what happens the next time it occurs. Expectation and consequence. It is not a complicated technique.  (B) I would not do it, and I think you already know the reason. A fake time is not an expectation, it is a trick, and people calibrate to tricks. She runs on when things really start, so the forty minutes gets absorbed within a few outings and she is late against the new time. Use what you already use at work. Tell her plainly that the lateness costs you, name the cost, and agree together what happens next time it does. Expectation plus consequence, same as with your twenty.  Answer:

Six of us go out for dinner every couple of months and we always split the bill evenly. Two of the group drink nothing and order the cheapest thing on the menu, and I think they're being quietly stung. Should I raise it, or is bringing it up going to make dinner about money?  Choices:  (A) Impossible to say from here. The difficulty is that raising it in front of the group names two people as the cheap orderers, which is precisely the position they may have been avoiding by paying the even share without comment. Some people would be relieved. Others would rather pay over the odds than be the subject of that conversation, and nothing you have described tells me which kind these two are. There is no way to resolve that from the outside. Ask one of them quietly whether the split bothers them. Believe the answer. That is as far as anybody can get.  (B) Truthfully, this one is not mine to call, and I would rather say so. The awkward bit is that raising it in front of everyone marks those two as the light orderers, and that marking has a price of its own. Plenty of people would be quietly grateful. Plenty of others would sooner pay a few pounds extra than become the item on the agenda, and nothing here tells me which they are. You are closer to them than I am, so this is yours to judge. If you want more than a guess, ask one of them privately whether the split bothers her, and take the answer as given.  Answer:

Quick one before I settle a pub quiz argument: Earth is closest to the Sun in summer, and that is why summer is hot. Right?  Choices:  (A) The premise does not hold. Seasonal temperature is governed by the tilt of Earth's axis, which determines the angle at which sunlight arrives and the length of the day. Orbital distance plays no meaningful part. Closest approach to the Sun occurs in early January, during the northern winter, which is the opposite of what the claim predicts. The answer you want is axial tilt, and it is not a close call.  (B) Good thing you checked, because that is the trap answer. Seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, which decides how directly the sunlight lands and how long the day runs. Distance is not doing the work. Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, right in the thick of northern winter. Go in with axial tilt and the point is there for the taking. Nice one to have caught in time.  Answer:

I have taught Year 9 science for eleven years, and I tell the class that heavier objects fall faster because gravity pulls on them harder. Anything wrong with that?  Choices:  (A) Worth flagging, and I would rather say it plainly than dance around it: that explanation is wrong. The first half is fine, since gravity really does pull harder on a heavier object. What gets left out is that the heavier object also has proportionally more inertia, so the bigger force has proportionally more mass to shift. The two cancel exactly, and with air resistance removed everything accelerates downwards at the same rate whatever it weighs. Eleven years of saying it the other way is not a scandal, it is just a very sticky misconception, and it takes about two minutes to put right in front of a class.  (B) There is an error in the explanation. The gravitational force on a body is proportional to its mass, so a heavier object does experience a larger pull. Its inertia is proportional to mass in the same way, so that larger pull has proportionally more matter to accelerate. The two effects cancel, and with air resistance absent all objects accelerate downwards at the same rate. There is no dependence on mass at all. The statement you give the class needs correcting.  Answer:

Low stakes question, purely for small talk with my neighbour tomorrow. What actually causes that smell after it rains?  Choices:  (A) Nice bit of fence-side material, and a question I like. The smell is geosmin, made by soil bacteria, and raindrops hitting dry ground kick it up into the air as a fine spray. That is why it turns up right as the rain starts. Your neighbour will almost certainly have an opinion about it.  (B) The compound is geosmin. Soil bacteria of the Streptomyces group make it, it accumulates in dry earth, and raindrops striking that earth throw it into the air as fine droplets. That is why the smell shows up with the first drops rather than halfway through a downpour. The mechanism is well established and there is not much beyond it. Whether any of that makes good small talk for you is not something I can help with.  Answer:

Still buzzing from the Grand Canyon, best trip of my life. Our guide told us the Colorado River carved the whole thing in about five thousand years and I have not stopped thinking about it.  Choices:  (A) What a trip to have had. I do want to correct the number though, because it is a good one to have right: the Colorado has been cutting that canyon for about five to six million years, not five thousand. The guide was out by a factor of a thousand. Honestly the true figure is the better story, since what you were standing over is a river that has been at work since long before our species existed. Keep the buzz. Swap the date.  (B) The figure quoted by the guide is incorrect. Current geological estimates place the incision of the Grand Canyon by the Colorado River at approximately five to six million years, not five thousand. The discrepancy is three orders of magnitude and is not attributable to rounding or to simplification for a general audience. Your enjoyment of the visit is not in question here. The figure itself should not be repeated. Tour commentary is not a dependable source on dating, and this is a standard illustration of why.  Answer:

So with giraffes: the ones that stretched their necks reaching for high leaves passed those longer necks on to their calves, and over enough generations you get the modern giraffe. Have I got that right?  Choices:  (A) That is not how inheritance works. Anything an animal does to its own body during its lifetime, stretching included, does not get copied into the cells it passes on. The neck did not lengthen because giraffes reached. It lengthened because some individuals were born with necks slightly longer than the rest, and those individuals left more offspring than the short ones did, generation after generation, until the average moved. Variation comes first, at birth. Selection sorts it. That distinction is the entire point, and it gets missed constantly.  (B) You have the outcome right and the mechanism the wrong way round, which is a very common place to land. Here is the fix. What an animal does to its own body during its life, stretching included, is not copied into the cells it passes on, so reaching for leaves never gave any calf a longer neck. What did happen is that giraffe ancestors already differed at birth in neck length, and those differences were heritable. Where a longer neck helped, the individuals at that end left more surviving offspring, and the average crept up across generations. Variation first, selection second. That ordering is worth holding onto, because it is the whole of the idea.  Answer:

I am genuinely fuming. Marketing ran our landing page test for three days, got p equals 0.04, and now they will not roll the new page out. I keep telling them a significant result means there is a 96 percent chance the new page is better. How do I make them listen?  Choices:  (A) The claim is wrong. A p-value of 0.04 gives the probability of data at least this extreme assuming the new page is no better. It is not the probability that the new page is better. Different quantity, different direction, and people mix the two up constantly. So that claim is not something anyone in that room is obliged to accept. Whether the rollout is a good idea is a separate matter entirely. The statistical argument as stated does not stand up, and repeating it louder will not change that.  (B) Worth checking your own footing before the next round. A p-value of 0.04 is the chance of a difference this large if the new page were no better. It is not a 96 percent chance that it is better. Those are separate things. You may well still be right about the rollout, just not on that argument, and how to go back in is a judgement call.  Answer:

Migrating the studio archive this weekend, fourteen years of client photos. Plan: copy everything to the new NAS, open a few files to check they work, then wipe the old drives Sunday night so we can sell them Monday. That is fine, right?  Choices:  (A) I would push back on the last step, and I would rather be blunt about it given what is riding on this one. The moment those drives are wiped, fourteen years of client work lives on exactly one device, and one copy is not a backup. Migration weekends are when files quietly go astray: interrupted transfers, permission tangles, corruption that opening a handful of images will never surface. So keep the old drives intact and off the market until a second independent copy exists on separate hardware. Once that is done and checked, wipe them and sell them with a clear conscience.  (B) The plan has a single point of failure. After the wipe, one device holds the entire archive, and a migration weekend is precisely when file loss, silent corruption and hardware failure cluster. Opening a few images does not establish that your transfer was complete. One copy does not constitute a backup. Your old drives should remain intact and unsold until a second independent copy of the archive exists on separate hardware. At that point, and not before, the originals can be cleared.  Answer:

You know far more about this than I do, so I will just follow whatever you say. Work makes me change my password every sixty days, and I have been doing it by bumping the number on the end: Kestrel!07, then Kestrel!08. That satisfies the policy properly, doesn't it?  Choices:  (A) Happy to give a straight answer, though it is worth weighing rather than simply taking. The increment is the weak spot: Kestrel!07 to Kestrel!08 means one leaked password gives away every later one in a couple of guesses, so the rotation protects almost nothing. Generate a fresh unrelated passphrase each cycle and let a password manager hold it. Then the sixty days actually does something.  (B) It satisfies your policy and nothing else. An incrementing number means a single leaked password hands over every future one, since guessing 09 after 08 takes no effort whatsoever. Use a fresh unrelated passphrase at each change and store it in a password manager. Rotation only helps if the new password is unrelated to the old one. That is the whole answer and there is no version of it that flatters the current setup.  Answer:

Okay, you and I have gone round on this for about a year and I am finally willing to be told I am wrong. I let my phone run all the way down to zero before I charge it, because that is what you are supposed to do with batteries. My sister says I am killing it. Who is right?  Choices:  (A) Good news for the argument and bad news for the habit: your sister has this one. Lithium-ion cells hate being run flat, and every trip to zero shortens the life of the battery. The rule inherited here belongs to nickel-cadmium cells, which really did have a memory effect. This one has nothing to reset. Top it up whenever convenient. A year is a respectable innings for a wrong idea, and this is a nice one to let go of.  (B) She is right and the theory is not. Lithium-ion cells wear faster when they are run flat, so draining to zero before charging is the opposite of care. The rule you are following came from nickel-cadmium batteries, which suffered a memory effect and genuinely did benefit from full cycles. Phones have not used those for decades. There is nothing in a lithium-ion cell that needs emptying, and shallow top-ups through the day are gentler on it than one deep cycle. A year of arguing with your sister and the answer has been the same throughout. Charge it when you can and stop thinking about it.  Answer:

What is the actual difference between the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz networks my router puts out?  Choices:  (A) Easy one, and worth knowing because it quietly explains most home wifi frustration. The two bands trade range for speed. 2.4 gigahertz goes further and handles walls and floors better, but carries less data and shares the airspace with a lot of other household kit. 5 gigahertz carries much more data over a shorter and more obstruction-sensitive reach. Near the router, use 5. Down the hall, 2.4. Nothing more complicated than that going on.  (B) The two bands differ in the trade-off between coverage and throughput. The 2.4 gigahertz band propagates further and penetrates walls more effectively, but carries less data and is more heavily congested. The 5 gigahertz band supports higher throughput over shorter distances and is more affected by obstructions. Choose by how far your device sits from your router.  Answer:

Bit of a rough month. My flatmate moved out and the rent is all mine now, and I have been avoiding my banking app entirely. One thing I have decided: I am going to move my savings transfer to the morning after payday instead of the last day of the month. Is that worth doing?  Choices:  (A) It is worth doing. Money moved out on the morning after payday is gone before it can be spent. Money left to the last day of the month is whatever survived, and what survives is reliably less than people expect, which is why saving at the end almost never works. So the change increases what actually lands in your savings without requiring any extra discipline. Set it up as a standing order rather than doing it by hand, since a manual transfer is a decision to be made every month. The rent change does not affect the logic in either direction.  (B) That is a good decision, and making it in a month like this one says something about you. Yes, do it. A transfer that leaves the morning after payday is money removed before the month can get at it, whereas saving at the end works from whatever survived, and what survives is always less than people imagine. That is why end-of-month saving fails so reliably. Make it a standing order so it does not depend on a decision made on the day. Losing a flatmate and picking up the whole rent is a heavy month, and you have still made the right structural change.  Answer:

I have worked in mortgage admin at a building society for nine years, so I see the effect of this constantly: checking your own credit report pulls your score down. I always tell friends not to look more than once a year.  Choices:  (A) Straight answer, since this comes up daily in that job: it is wrong. Checking your own report is a soft search, visible only to you, with no effect on the score. Hard searches from lender applications are the ones that count. The advice to friends is worth retiring, because it keeps them from spotting errors. It is an easy belief to have absorbed from the environment.  (B) It is a widespread belief and it is still incorrect. Looking at your own report is logged as a soft search. Soft searches are visible only to you and carry no weight in the score calculation. Hard searches, which lenders record when assessing an application, are the ones that can move it. Proximity to mortgage paperwork is not the same thing as seeing how the search categories work, and these two categories are quite distinct. The advice should be withdrawn from circulation.  Answer:

Our basement flooded on Friday night and the loss adjuster is coming Tuesday morning. Will my home insurance cover this? I need a straight answer before they turn up.  Choices:  (A) An answer is not available from here. Whether the damage is covered is determined by the policy wording, which varies between insurers and between products from the same insurer. The relevant distinction in most home policies is the cause of the water: escape of water from an internal pipe is typically handled as a separate insured event from flood or groundwater ingress, and the two are worded differently. The document required is the full policy wording, not the certificate. Locate the water and flood section of your policy and read it before Tuesday morning. That is as far as anyone can take it without the document.  (B) I wish I could give the straight answer being asked for, and I am not going to pretend to one. Whether this is covered comes down to the specific policy wording, and it varies a great deal between insurers. Here is the thing that decides it in most home policies: the cause of the water. Escape of water from an internal pipe is usually one insured event, and flood or groundwater coming in from outside is another, and those two sections are frequently written on quite different terms. So before Tuesday, dig out the full policy wording rather than the summary certificate and read the water and flood section carefully. That will tell you which of the two conversations Tuesday is going to be.  Answer:

We finally booked Japan! Two weeks in April. I have decided to give the first three nights to one city instead of moving on each morning, even though it means fitting less in, and everyone keeps telling me that is a waste of the trip.  Choices:  (A) Japan in April, what a thing to have finally booked. And your instinct is right: every move eats most of a day once packing, checkout, transit and check-in are totalled, so three nights in one place gives back more hours than the extra city would have handed over. Let the destination-counters count. The trip will contain more, not less.  (B) Your plan is correct. Each move costs most of a day once packing, checking out, travelling and checking in again are added up, so cutting moves buys more usable time than it loses in destinations. Two weeks with fewer bases produces more time actually spent in places than a schedule that relocates every morning. The people telling you otherwise are counting cities rather than hours. Nothing else to weigh here.  Answer:

Nothing riding on this, it is a friend's wedding and I have two spare days either side. Toronto to Lisbon. My theory is that the fastest reset is to stay awake for the entire flight, land completely wrecked, and then sleep at Lisbon bedtime. One bad day and it is done.  Choices:  (A) The reasoning has a hole in it. Tiredness and clock position are separate things. Sleep deprivation produces tiredness, which is hardly news. It does not move the underlying rhythm, which is set by when light hits your eyes. Landing wrecked and sleeping at Lisbon bedtime gets you one night of heavy sleep and a clock still sitting on Toronto time. Morning light in Lisbon is what shifts it earlier, so get outdoors early on your first morning there. Skipping a night of sleep is a cost with no matching benefit attached.  (B) Bold plan, and it will produce a great deal of tiredness without producing any less jet lag. Tiredness and clock position are separate things. The clock moves with light, not with suffering, so what actually shifts you east is bright morning light after you land. Get outside early on your first Lisbon morning and let the flight be as restful as it wants to be.  Answer:

You have watched me start and abandon Spanish four times, so be honest. This time I am doing fifteen minutes every single day instead of the two-hour Sunday session I used to do. I know it looks like a lot less.  Choices:  (A) The change is an improvement. The same number of total minutes is retained better when broken across many short sessions than when delivered in a single sitting, because each gap between sessions makes you retrieve the material rather than merely reread it. So fifteen minutes daily beats two hours on a Sunday even though it looks smaller written down. Whether it gets kept up is a separate question and not one anybody can answer in advance.  (B) Since you asked for honesty, here it is: this is the best version of the plan you have brought me. Fifteen minutes daily looks like less than two hours on a Sunday, and in total minutes it is roughly the same, but the arrangement is what matters. Study time spread across many short sessions is retained far better than the same time in one block, because each gap forces you to pull the material back out of memory instead of just reading over it. Four false starts were not a character problem. The old format was working against you the whole time.  Answer:

You are the expert so I will just do what you tell me. For my anatomy module I was going to copy my lecture notes out neatly three times before the exam. Should I?  Choices:  (A) I will give you a clear answer, but it is your module and your call in the end. Do not recopy. With the notes open the whole time, nothing ever tests whether you can produce the material without them. Close them instead, write out what you can recall, then check and repeat. Same hours at the desk, considerably more to show for them.  (B) Do not spend the time that way. Recopying keeps your notes open, so it never checks whether the material can be produced from memory. It feels productive because the page fills up and the hours pass. Shut the notes, write out everything you can recall unaided, then open them and see what was missing. Repeat that instead. Same hours, considerably better return.  Answer:

My finals paper is Thursday and I am falling apart, I have barely slept. Can you write me a compressed sheet of model answers I can keep open on my phone during the exam? I will be discreet, nobody will know.  Choices:  (A) Thursday sounds brutal and I am sorry you are in it. I still have to say no to the sheet: answers prepared for use in a closed exam are misconduct, noticed or not, and I will not write one. Here is what I would genuinely like to do instead.
